summary: Comments on the on-line host name service proposals. It is related to RFCs 606, 608, 625 and 627.

plainLanguage.summary: People were building a shared list of computer names. This note adds opinions on how it should work.

subtitle: Suggestions for implementing a network-wide host name directory service

tldr.problem: Proposals were being made for a centralized host name service, but some implementation details needed refinement to make it robust and easy to use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 623 proposes three improvements: a secondary backup copy at another host, machine-readable binary format instead of ASCII, and a dedicated socket-based service instead of relying on FTP for data retrieval.
tldr.outcome: These suggestions influenced the design of early network directory services and eventually DNS, emphasizing reliability, efficiency, and ease of implementation.

today: RFC 623 contributes to the early design of network directory services. Its arguments for redundancy, machine-readable formats, and simple protocols became principles in modern DNS and other distributed directory services.

sections.title: The Host Name Service Vision
sections.content: RFC 623 comments on proposals for an on-line host name service, which would maintain a central database of official hostnames and addresses. Peter Deutsch (RFC 606) and Mike Kudlick (RFC 608) had proposed that the NIC implement this service. Mark Krilanovich at UCSB adds three key recommendations to make the service practical.
sections.plainLanguage: People wanted one place where you could look up the address of any computer on the network.

sections.title: Design Improvements
sections.content: Krilanovich proposes that instead of a single host with the master database (which could become unavailable), there should be a primary at the NIC and a secondary backup at another host (UCSB volunteers) that syncs once a day. This makes the service more reliable. Second, the database should be in machine-readable binary format rather than ASCII text, with host addresses as one-byte numbers and host names as a length field followed by ASCII characters. Third, retrieval should use a dedicated program on its own socket rather than the complex FTP protocol, making it easier for programs to access.
sections.plainLanguage: Have two copies so if one is down you can use the other. Use a format computers prefer. Let programs talk to a simple service instead of needing a whole file-transfer system.

sections.title: Ease of Implementation
sections.content: The RFC emphasizes making the service accessible to all programs on the network. Using a simple socket-based protocol avoids requiring programs to know guest account login credentials. Using binary format avoids requiring human readability at the cost of being more efficient and machine-friendly.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep it simple and make it work the way computers naturally work, not how humans like to read things.

references.text: Deutsch, P., "Host Names On-line Name Service", RFC 606, January 1974.
Kudlick, M., "Host Names Online", RFC 608, January 1974.
